items.title: Pineapples photosynthesise at night
items.claim: Most plants open their stomata in daytime to take in CO2 and lose water to evaporation. CAM plants (crassulacean acid metabolism — cacti, pineapples, agaves) keep stomata SHUT all day and open them only at night, storing CO2 as malic acid for the day's photosynthesis.
items.prompt: Why would a plant fix CO2 in the dark?

options.text: By separating CO2 uptake (cool, humid night) from light reactions (hot, dry day), CAM plants cut water loss by 80-90% versus C3 plants — essential in deserts where transpiration would be lethal

items.reveal:
C3 plants (wheat, rice, ~85% of species): Rubisco fixes CO2 directly in mesophyll cells. Simple, but loses water and suffers photorespiration when hot.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum): PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into a 4-carbon acid (oxaloacetate) in mesophyll cells. The acid is shipped to bundle-sheath cells, where Rubisco operates in a CO2-rich environment. About 3% of species, but include some of the most productive crops.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples, succulents, agaves): same chemistry as C4 but separated in TIME instead of space. Stomata open at night; CO2 is stored as malic acid in vacuoles; daylight releases it for Rubisco.

Each is a different trade-off between water loss, productivity and temperature tolerance. C4 and CAM evolved independently dozens of times — convergent solutions to Rubisco's flaws.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as a single process. In reality, plants have invented three biochemically distinct strategies, each suited to a different climate.

items.title: Sugar in plants flows from wherever it's made to wherever it's needed
items.claim: Xylem carries water in one direction: up. Phloem carries dissolved sugars in any direction — up, down, lateral — from 'sources' (leaves, storage organs being mobilised) to 'sinks' (roots, fruits, growing tips). The same phloem tube can reverse direction with the season.

options.text: Pressure-flow (Munch) hypothesis: sugar loaded at the source raises osmotic pressure there, drawing in water from xylem; unloaded sugar at the sink reduces pressure; bulk flow proceeds from high to low pressure along the phloem

items.reveal:
Phloem sieve tubes are living cells (unlike xylem vessels, which are dead). Companion cells help load sugar into sieve elements at sources.

Loading: at a source (e.g., a photosynthesising leaf), sucrose is actively pumped INTO sieve elements via H+/sucrose symporters. Sucrose concentration rises to 1 mol/L. Water enters by osmosis. Hydrostatic pressure builds.

Unloading: at a sink (a fruit, root, or growing meristem), sucrose is removed and metabolised or stored. Water exits. Pressure drops.

The pressure gradient pushes sap from source to sink at ~1 metre/hour — much slower than xylem flow but still bulk flow.

Direction reverses seasonally. In spring, a deciduous tree's stored root sugars are sources, mobilising to buds (sinks). In summer, leaves are sources, fruits and roots are sinks. In autumn, leaves dump sugars to storage organs before falling.

Aphids tap phloem with their stylets and benefit from the natural pressure — sap is forced out of them as honeydew. Scientists use severed aphid stylets as natural phloem sampling needles.
items.why: Plant transport feels static. The phloem is a dynamic, switchable distribution network with pressure-driven bulk flow — and it can reverse direction within a single growing season.

items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.
